body:
Part A:
Below you are given a Question and a Possible Answer. Go over the Answer step-by-step and grade it, pointing out mistakes (if any) and praising clever steps (if any).
Question: Let \(X_i\sim IIDN(\mu,\sigma^2)\), \(i=1,2,\ldots,n\). Define \[ \overline X=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i}{n} \qquad\text{and}\qquad S^2=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\overline X)^2. \] Show that \(\dfrac{nS^2}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2_{n-1}\).
Answer: We can write \[ \begin{aligned} \sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\overline X)^2 &=\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl[(X_i-\mu)-(\overline X-\mu)\bigr]^2\\ &=\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\mu)^2+n(\overline X-\mu)^2 -2\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\mu)(\overline X-\mu)\\ &=\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\mu)^2+n(\overline X-\mu)^2, \end{aligned} \] the last term being zero since \(X_i\)'s are independent.
Therefore, \[\frac{nS^2}{\sigma^2} =\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\frac{X_i-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2 +\frac{n(\overline X-\mu)^2}{\sigma^2}. \tag{1}\] Now \[ \sum_{i=1}^n\left(\frac{X_i-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2\sim\chi_n^2 \] and \[ \frac{n(\overline X-\mu)^2}{\sigma^2} =\frac{(\overline X-\mu)^2}{\sigma^2/n}\sim\chi_1^2, \qquad\text{since }\overline X\sim N\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right). \] Thus going back to the equation (1) above, we clearly see that \(\dfrac{nS^2}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi_{n-1}^2\). Q.E.D.

(i) Let \(X_i\sim\mathrm{IIDN}(\mu,\sigma^2)\), \(i=1,2,\ldots,n\).
Define \[ \overline X=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i}{n} \qquad\text{and}\qquad S^{\prime 2}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(X_i-\overline X)^2}{n-1}. \] Find \(E(\overline X)\), \(E(S^{\prime 2})\), \(Var(\overline X)\), and \(Var(S^{\prime 2})\).
(ii) Now relax the independence assumption: Let \(Corr(X_i,X_j)=\rho>0\), \(i\neq j\). Now find \(E(\overline X)\), \(E(S^{\prime 2})\) and \(Var(\overline X)\).
(iii) Interpret the differences (if any) in the expressions of \(Var(\overline X)\) in (i) and (ii).

title: A Little Theory
body:

body:

body:
Given a random sample \(\{X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n\}\) from the population \(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), define \[ \overline X=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n X_i}{n}, \qquad S^2=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\overline X)^2, \] \[ S^{\prime 2}=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\overline X)^2 \quad\text{and}\quad S_0^2=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\mu)^2. \]
In the class, we proved that \(\overline X\) and \(S^2\) are independent, and they are distributed as, respectively, \[ \overline X\sim N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right), \qquad \frac{nS^2}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2_{n-1}. \]

Grade the Answer to the following Question.

\textbf{Question:} Let $y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_{10}$ denote a random sample of size 10 from a Poisson distribution with mean $\lambda$. $H_0:\lambda=0.1$ against $\lambda=0.5$. Find the best critical region, for a significance level of $\alpha=0.05$.

\textbf{Hint:} When $X$ has a Poisson distribution with mean $\lambda=1.0$, following Table gives $\Pr(X\leq r)$:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{c|ccccccc}
$r$ & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 \\ \hline
$\Pr(X\leq r)$ & .378 & .736 & .920 & .981 & .996 & .999 & 1.000
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\textbf{Answer:} Use the likelihood ratio test. Let us denote $H_0:\lambda=\lambda_0$ and $H_a:\lambda=\lambda_1$. Then
\[
L(\lambda_0)=\frac{e^{-n\lambda_0}\lambda_0^{\sum_{i=1}^{10}y_i}}{\prod_{i=1}^{10}y_i!}
\]
and
\[
L(\lambda_1)=\frac{e^{-n\lambda_1}\lambda_1^{\sum_{i=1}^{10}y_i}}{\prod_{i=1}^{10}y_i!}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\frac{L(\lambda_0)}{L(\lambda_1)}
=e^{-n(\lambda_0-\lambda_1)}\left[\frac{\lambda_0}{\lambda_1}\right]^{\sum_{i=1}^{10}y_i}.
\]
Best critical region will be obtained from
\[
\frac{L(\lambda_0)}{L(\lambda_1)}<k,
\qquad\text{where }k\text{ is a constant}
\]
or $\sum_{i=1}^{10}y_i\geq c$ where $c$ is a constant. We have to choose $c$ in such a way that the significance level $\alpha=.05$ i.e.,
\[
\Pr\left(\sum_{i=1}^{10}y_i\geq c\mid H_0\right)=.05
\]
or
\[
\Pr\left(\sum_{i=1}^{10}y_i\geq c\mid\lambda=.1\right)=.05.
\]
Since $y_i$ follows Poisson with mean $.1$, for $i=1,2,\ldots,10$, $\sum_{i=1}^{10}y_i$ follows Poisson with mean $10\times .1=1$. From the Poisson probability table given in the Hint, get $c=4$. Hence the best critical region is given by $\sum_{i=1}^{10}y_i\geq4$.

Answer: Since \(T\) is sufficient for \(\theta\), the conditional expectation of \(T_1\) given \(T=t\) is independent of \(\theta\). Thus \(h(t)\) is independent of \(\theta\). Using the result of conditional expectation, we see that \[E(T_1)=E[E(T_1\mid T)]=E[h(T)] \tag{1}\] which shows that \(T_1\) and \(h(T)\) have the same expectation. Furthermore, \[\begin{aligned} E\{h(T)[T_1-h(T)]\} &=E\{h(T)[E(T_1-h(T)\mid T)]\} \\ &=0,\quad\text{since }E(T_1\mid T=t)=h(t). \end{aligned}\tag{2}\] Consider \[\begin{aligned} E[T_1-g(\theta)]^2 &=E[T_1-h(T)+h(T)-g(\theta)]^2 \\ &=E[T_1-h(T)]^2+E[h(T)-g(\theta)]^2 \\ &\geq E[h(T)-g(\theta)]^2, \end{aligned}\tag{3}\] since the product term \[\begin{aligned}E[T_1-h(T)][h(T)-g(\theta)] &=E\{[T_1-h(T)]h(T)\}-g(\theta)E[T_1-h(T)]\\ &=0-0=0,\end{aligned}\] if we use (1) and (2). The equality in (3) is attained only when \(T_1=h(T)\). From (1), \(E[h(T)]=g(\theta)\) if \(E(T_1)=g(\theta)\).
